claims.text: Rapidly quenched FeCoNiTi forms a dual-phase microstructure consisting of an fcc matrix and a hexagonal C14 Laves phase.
The fcc matrix in the dual-phase FeCoNiTi alloy is ferromagnetic.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys have coercivity below or capped near 100 Oe because their orbital moments are limited.
Rapid quenching stabilizes the dual-phase fcc/C14 microstructure in FeCoNiTi.
A continuous or semi-continuous C14 interfacial network is sufficient to substantially influence the alloy's magnetic response.
Ti occupies an atomic arrangement in the C14 Laves phase that facilitates exchange coupling with adjacent fcc Fe, Co, and Ni atoms.
The C14 phase in FeCoNiTi is Ti-rich.
Ti in the C14 phase carries local antiferromagnetic moments or induces strong spin fluctuations.
Ti-associated moments or spin fluctuations in the C14 phase couple antiparallel to the ferromagnetic Fe-Co-Ni moments in the fcc phase.
Interfacial antiferromagnetic coupling suppresses the effective saturation magnetization of the fcc phase.
The fcc/C14 interfaces generate high local magnetic-anisotropy barriers that pin domain walls.
Domain-wall pinning and interfacial anisotropy increase coercivity above the intrinsic coercivity of single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni.
Replacing half of the ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr in AlCoFeNi lowers saturation magnetization to 42.2 emu/g and raises coercivity to 39.4 Oe.
Phase decomposition into a B2 matrix and fine Fe-Co-rich BCC precipitates in AlCoFeNi is associated with lower saturation magnetization and higher coercivity.
The dual-phase FeCoNiTi alloy will have a coercivity of approximately 667 Oe at 400 K.
The dual-phase FeCoNiTi alloy will have lower saturation magnetization than a corresponding single-phase fcc alloy.

Spin-polarized DFT calculations comparing an isolated fcc phase with an fcc/C14 slab can test changes in the fcc spin density of states at the Fermi level and calculate interfacial exchange-coupling energy.
Direct comparison of dual-phase and single-phase FeCoNiTi hysteresis loops at 400 K can test whether the C14 phase is necessary for enhanced coercivity.
